results.summary: This project creates generative cross-stitch patterns using the metal layers of the silicon die. It has no electrical function; the only pin is a dummy output. The design is purely artistic and requires no external hardware. It is notable for using the chip as a canvas for visual art rather than computation.

This project implements a two-player Pong game that outputs to a VGA monitor and accepts input from two NES controllers. The NES controllers connect via three wires each to the bidirectional pins, and the VGA signals are output on the dedicated output pins. External hardware needed includes two NES controllers, a VGA breakout board (such as the Tiny Tapeout VGA PMOD), and a VGA-compatible monitor. The design is notable for combining classic gaming with retro controllers and a standard video interface.

This is a 2-bit flash analog-to-digital converter that converts an analog input voltage between 0 and 1.8V into a 2-bit digital code. The analog input is applied to a dedicated analog pin, and the encoded outputs appear on two digital output pins. No external hardware is required beyond the analog voltage source. The design is notable for being a compact, purely analog implementation of a flash ADC.

This project implements an 8x8 unsigned Braun array multiplier that computes the product of two 8-bit numbers and outputs a 16-bit result. The inputs are provided on the input and bidirectional pins, and the product is output on the output and bidirectional pins. The design is purely combinational and does not require a clock or external hardware. It is notable for its low-power array architecture and systematic use of full and half adders.

This project implements a 4-bit Brent-Kung adder that takes two 4-bit inputs and a carry-in, producing a 5-bit sum output. The design is combinational and can be tested using a provided Verilog testbench with Icarus Verilog and GTKWave. No external hardware is required for operation. The project is notable for being a quick implementation of a parallel prefix adder, likely created in a short time frame.

This project implements a simple direct-mapped cache memory controller that manages four cache blocks. It accepts an 8-bit address and a read/write signal on the input pins and returns 8-bit data on the output pins. The design is synchronous and includes simulation testbenches and cocotb tests for verification. It is notable for fitting a basic cache controller into a single Tiny Tapeout tile.

This project implements a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron using 8-bit signed Q4.4 fixed-point arithmetic. It integrates an input current, applies a leak, and emits a spike when the membrane potential exceeds a threshold, with a programmable refractory period. The design is intended for tapeout and uses only adds, subtracts, and shifts. Testing requires an external ADALM2000 for stimulus and observation.

This project implements a combinational logic-based pipeline hazard resolution unit for a RISC-V processor. It detects control, data, and structural hazards and generates signals to freeze the program counter, flush the pipeline, and indicate hazard-free execution. The design is tested in simulation by applying hazard scenarios and observing state transitions. It is self-contained and requires only a clock and reset, with no external hardware needed.

This project implements a custom arithmetic logic unit (ALU) that also supports neural-inspired operations in a separate NPU mode. It takes two 4-bit operands and a 4-bit opcode plus a mode bit to select from operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, bitwise logic, rotation, priority encoding, gray code conversion, majority, and various neural computations. The 8-bit output includes the result and error, sign, carry, and zero flags. The design is purely combinational and requires no external hardware.

This project implements a current-mode bandgap reference that provides a PVT-stable 1V reference voltage and a 5.6uA reference current. It includes a test buffer for measurement, an 8-bit trim for process variation, and SPI control for configuration. Testing requires a 3.3V supply, a ~5uA bias current for the test buffer, and a multimeter to measure voltage and current. Silicon tests confirm the voltage buffer and reference are working, with a 1V output at a trim value of 142.
